observation: The 125 founder-decided rules became the ACCEPTANCE TEST for a 15-clause engine instead of 125 hand-written rules. A mutation test killed 12 of 12 single-clause mutants. Compressing a decision artifact into principles, then using the decisions as the regression net, is the pattern to repeat.

Three review rounds, and each one found the SAME defect class in a place the previous fix had not reached: a detector resolved `const t = teams` but the publication-side rule did not, so `export const betsTable = bets` defeated the table ACL; the table detector resolved const aliases but the spawn detector did not, so `const CLI = "claude"` defeated the one-door rule. Fixing a class on one side of a boundary and not the other is the recurring shape.

I committed a RED tree while my own lint said green. The census read `git ls-files`, which cannot see unstaged files, so I recomputed a floor against a census missing the four rule files I was about to commit. The adversarial review had already named this exact divergence and I did not act on it. Fixed at the source: trackedFiles now reads --cached --others --exclude-standard.

CI was broken on the branch and nobody noticed until a reviewer swept `.github/`. Ruling 10 deleted a guard script and left release-guard.yml invoking it. Every local gate was green. This is the strongest possible argument for the founder's rule that green means CI green — the local suite cannot see a workflow file.

A real security hole shipped in docs as a met requirement: the desktop app was documented as binding localhost only and actually bound `::` — reachable from the LAN. Fixed the code rather than the doc. The test then caught a SECOND bug in the fix (a hostname routes listen() through async DNS even for a literal IP, so desktop would have thrown on every launch). Writing the test first is what caught it.

Transcribed counts in prose rotted THREE times, the third inside the commit that fixed the second. Updating them was the wrong fix each time. The right fix, applied on round three, was to DELETE every transcribed number and keep only the reasoning — the enforced constants are the record and a prose copy is pure liability.

The founder's reframing of what a linter is FOR re-sorted the entire finding list in one sentence: guidance not anti-malice, must catch a different implementation STYLE. Five of six bypasses became must-fix; eslint-disable, untracked files and template-interpolated imports were rejected by name as theatre. Without that frame I would have built anti-malice machinery and still missed the aliased import.

Break-testing became a gate, not a one-off: 47 attacks overlaid onto the LIVE census through the readFile seam, inside npm run lint. The property that makes it durable is that a registered rule with no POSITIVE attack case fails the build. Round 2 found the first version was satisfiable by a control twin — and fixing that exposed that the only crossing-event case emitted an undeclared event type, so it was clean for the wrong reason and would have stayed clean with the detector deleted.

Every sweep I ran was rigorous INSIDE a scope I never questioned. The doc sweep covered docs/ and missed .github/. The path sweep checked files exist and missed whether line numbers point at the right code. The symbol sweep checked names and missed names surviving only in comments. The floor recompute fixed the constant and missed the prose two lines below. A reviewer named it: this is the same shape as the original AU28 bug — a guard that checked one direction of one pair, thoroughly.

Twice I pointed readers at a document I had not opened. The docs rewrite replaced 45 partly-stale lines with a pointer to a doc that documented four guards this branch had deleted — a net regression, in a commit titled 'fix the docs that lie'.

A symbol-list sweep reported '0 dead symbols' while three live falsehoods survived, because their names were not on the list. A name-list check only finds names on the list. The passes that caught real problems read prose against code instead.

Delegating review to four independent hostile agents found what I could not: six proven bypasses with working reproductions, two failed ACs, and a docs regression. The producer cannot review their own work — every round of this proved it again. Two reviewers independently found the same CI break from different starting points, which is what made it credible immediately.

Builders were told to prove each fix by temporarily REVERTING it and watching the break-test go red, never by assertion. That discipline caught a plan error (the stated mechanism for the alias fix would not have worked — the census records the original name, not the local alias) and attributed a metric drop correctly (di 257->245 was real code deletion by this branch's own purge, confirmed by counting at the commit and diffing the sets, not assumed).

Two ENTIRE eslint rules and five more `files:` patterns matched zero files — the au6 shape, found seven more times inside the work package built to eliminate it. A pattern that matches nothing is a silent no-op that reads as enforcement forever.

The stale compiled .js hazard bit twice in one day: a composite build emits .js beside .ts, node/tsx/vitest resolve the compiled copy first, so the guard ran OLD logic while the source said otherwise. tsc hides the cause as TS6059. Now closed by a rule plus gate cleanup.

scripts/ — the home of the governance guard — was never typechecked. A missing import in governance-lint.ts passed npm run check. The tooling that enforces correctness sat outside the correctness net. Added scripts/tsconfig.json and wired the gate.

My first two negative controls were FALSE — they used a specifier that resolved to nothing, so 'no violation detected' looked like a pass when the probe never fired. A negative control that cannot fire manufactures confidence.

Ruling 13a came from retesting a discriminator instead of accepting the founder's framing that 91 violations were 'an easy fix'. The derivable criterion — does the owner ever REVISE the row — removed 51 false positives with zero test edits. An append-only log is history, not state.

Founder questions caught two things four hostile reviewers missed. 'gh is used by the filesystem I assume not as a harness?' exposed a category error I had relayed uncorrected. Then 'what the agent can reach is permissions or filesystem not harness' exposed a structural misfiling — inheritedTools hanging off the harness descriptor. Registered as AU36.

I ran the retro while review said NOT DONE. The founder corrected the order: iterate -> review DONE -> human review -> retro -> ship. A mid-iteration retro also records defects the fix cycle then closes, so it documents a state that no longer exists by the time anyone reads it. Deleted and re-run at the end.

Parallel agents writing to one worktree nearly collided: an adversarial reviewer had scratch files STAGED IN THE INDEX while another agent read the tree, and a later builder clobbered a file with git checkout and hand-reconstructed it. No damage, but a commit during either window would have captured it. Parallel writers need tree ownership, not just scope separation.

Parallelising the docs rewrite across three agents was fast but produced inconsistent editorial voice — two narrated deletions as history instead of deleting, violating the explicit 'delete rather than hedge' instruction. A fourth agent re-verifying the other three caught it, plus a bad path in its own earlier work. Self-review of delegated work is worth its cost.

Net -2,007 lines: twenty inherited guards deleted against 15 rules added. I had framed this as a ~9,000-line addition until a reviewer measured it — the framing changes whether the size is itself a finding.

Rulings 14 and 15 came from the founder noticing the vocabulary was wrong, not the code: raw runtime and harness were two names for one act, and harness had been stretched to cover a GitHub CLI auth probe. Merging them fixed a live contradiction where a test importing the OpenAI SDK was blocked while a test spawning claude was waved through.
